questions.question: Two sealed-bid formats for $n$ bidders both satisfy the revenue equivalence theorem's hypotheses (risk-neutral bidders, i.i.d. private values with CDF $F$ on $[\underline\theta,\overline\theta]$, an equilibrium always allocating to the highest value, zero expected surplus for the lowest type $\underline\theta$). Which quantity is guaranteed equal in the two equilibria?
options: The expected payment $m(\theta)$ of each type $\theta$
The bid $b(\theta)$ submitted by each type $\theta$
The winner's price in every realization of values
The shading $\theta-b(\theta)$ of each type $\theta$

questions.question: In the revenue equivalence theorem, $n$ bidders have i.i.d. private values with CDF $F$, and the equilibrium always gives the object to the highest value. What does $G(\theta)=F(\theta)^{n-1}$ represent?
options: The probability that the highest of all $n$ values is at most $\theta$
The probability that at least one of the $n-1$ rivals has a lower value
The expected amount that type $\theta$ pays to the seller in equilibrium
The probability that type $\theta$ wins: all $n-1$ rivals are lower

questions.question: With two bidders whose values are i.i.d. $U[0,1]$, the revenue equivalence theorem needs an equilibrium in which the object always goes to the bidder with the higher value. Which equilibrium satisfies this condition?
options: A second-price auction in which bidder 1 always bids $1$ and bidder 2 always bids $0$
A second-price auction with reserve price $\frac{1}{2}$ and truthful bids
A first-price auction in which both bidders bid $\theta/2$
A lottery handing the object to a randomly drawn bidder for free

questions.question: Two risk-neutral bidders have i.i.d. $U[0,1]$ values, so $G(\theta)=\theta$, and a format satisfies the revenue equivalence theorem's hypotheses. Using $U(\theta)=\int_0^{\theta}G(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$, what is the equilibrium expected surplus of type $\theta=0.6$?

Three risk-neutral bidders have i.i.d. $U[0,1]$ values and a format satisfies the revenue equivalence theorem's hypotheses. Using $m(\theta)=\theta G(\theta)-\int_0^{\theta}G(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ with $G=F^{n-1}$, what is the equilibrium expected payment $m(\theta)$?
options: $\theta^3$
$\frac{2}{3}\theta^3$
$\frac{1}{3}\theta^3$
$\frac{3}{4}\theta^4$

questions.question: Two bidders have values $\theta_1=0.9$ and $\theta_2=0.2$, drawn i.i.d. from $U[0,1]$. In the first-price auction both bid $\theta/2$; in the second-price auction both bid their values. What revenue does the seller actually collect in each format for these values?
options: First-price $0.2$, second-price $0.2$
First-price $0.1$, second-price $0.2$
First-price $0.45$, second-price $0.2$
First-price $0.9$, second-price $0.2$

questions.question: Three bidders have i.i.d. $U[0,1]$ values. In the first-price equilibrium a type $\theta=0.9$ bids $0.6$ and wins with probability $0.81$. By the revenue equivalence theorem, what is this type's expected payment in the truthful second-price equilibrium?

Two risk-neutral bidders have i.i.d. $U[0,1]$ values. A seller runs a second-price auction with reserve price $r=\frac{1}{2}$: the object is sold only if some bid is at least $\frac{1}{2}$. Which hypothesis of the revenue equivalence theorem fails when this is compared with a first-price auction without reserve?
options: The lowest type no longer has zero surplus, since it must pay the reserve
The object no longer always goes to the highest value, since it can stay unsold
Values are no longer private, since the reserve acts as a known rival value
Bidders are no longer risk-neutral, since an unsold object adds risk

questions.question: Bidder 1's value is uniform on $[0,1]$ and bidder 2's value, independently, is uniform on $[0,2]$; both are risk-neutral. Why may the revenue equivalence theorem fail to equate the first-price and second-price auctions here?
options: Values stop being private, since each bidder's range is informative about the other
The lowest type's surplus becomes positive, because bidder 2's values can exceed $1$
Values are not identically distributed, so first-price bids can favour the lower value
Risk neutrality fails, because bidder 2 faces a wider spread of possible values

questions.question: For $n$ risk-neutral bidders with i.i.d. private values, formats A and B use the same efficient allocation in equilibrium. In A the lowest type has expected surplus $0$; B also pays every bidder a fixed amount $k>0$ regardless of bids, so its lowest type gets $k$. How do expected revenues compare?
options: B earns $k$ less than A: only the winner's transfer
Revenues are equal, as the allocation is the same
B earns $nk$ less than A: one $k$ per bidder
B earns $kG(\theta)$ less per type: only winners get $k$

questions.question: Three bidders have i.i.d. $U[0,1]$ values, and in every format satisfying the revenue equivalence theorem a type $\theta$ pays $m(\theta)=\frac{2}{3}\theta^3$ in expectation. What is one bidder's ex ante expected payment $\mathbb{E}[m(\theta)]$, before her value is drawn?

In an all-pay auction every bidder pays her own bid whether she wins or not, and the highest bid wins. Five risk-neutral bidders have i.i.d. $U[0,1]$ values and the symmetric increasing equilibrium meets the revenue equivalence hypotheses. What is the equilibrium bid $b(\theta)$?
options: $\frac{4}{5}\theta$
$\frac{1}{5}\theta^5$
$\frac{4}{25}\theta^5$
$\frac{4}{5}\theta^5$

questions.question: Five risk-neutral bidders have i.i.d. $U[0,1]$ values. In a sealed-bid format the highest bid wins and pays the average of her bid and the second-highest bid; losers pay nothing. Assume a symmetric equilibrium with strictly increasing bids. What is the seller's expected revenue?
options: $\frac{3}{4}$, the average of the expected top two values
$\frac{2}{3}$, the expected second-highest value
$\frac{5}{6}$, the expected highest value
No value until the bidding function is solved

questions.question: The revenue equivalence theorem assumes risk-neutral bidders, i.i.d. private values, an equilibrium allocating to the highest value, and zero surplus for the lowest type. If one hypothesis fails for some format, what follows about its expected revenue relative to the truthful second-price auction?
options: Nothing in general: the hypotheses are sufficient, so the comparison is left open
It must differ, since each hypothesis is necessary for equal expected revenue
It must be lower, since breaking a hypothesis always costs the seller revenue
It is still equal provided the bidders remain risk-neutral

questions.question: With risk-averse instead of risk-neutral bidders (i.i.d. private values), the first-price auction raises more expected revenue than the second-price auction. Which mechanism explains this ranking?
options: Second-price bidders shade below value, while first-price bids are unchanged
Risk-averse first-price bidders bid their full value to avoid the risk of losing
Risk aversion lowers bids in both formats, but by more in the second-price auction
Second-price truthful bidding stays weakly dominant; first-price bidders shade less

questions.question: Two risk-neutral bidders have i.i.d. values with CDF $F(\theta)=\theta^2$ on $[0,1]$. Using revenue equivalence, a type-$\theta$ first-price bidder pays $b(\theta)$ with probability $G(\theta)$, so $b(\theta)=m(\theta)/G(\theta)$ with $m(\theta)=\theta G(\theta)-\int_0^\theta G(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$. What is the first-price equilibrium bid?
options: $\frac{1}{2}\theta$
$\frac{2}{3}\theta^3$
$\frac{4}{5}\theta$
$\frac{2}{3}\theta$

questions.question: Two risk-neutral bidders have i.i.d. values with CDF $F(\theta)=\theta^2$ on $[0,1]$, and an auction format satisfies the revenue equivalence theorem's hypotheses. Using $\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_0^1\mathbb{P}(X>x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ for a value $X$ in $[0,1]$, what is the seller's expected revenue?

The revenue equivalence theorem states that expected revenue equals $\mathbb{E}[\theta_{(n-1)}]$, where $\theta_{(1)}\le\theta_{(2)}\le\cdots\le\theta_{(n)}$ are the $n$ bidders' values sorted from smallest to largest. Which description of $\theta_{(n-1)}$ is correct for every number of bidders $n\ge2$?
options: The second-highest of the $n$ values
The second-lowest of the $n$ values
The value of the bidder labelled $n-1$
The highest value among bidder 1's $n-1$ rivals

questions.question: In an auction format satisfying the hypotheses of the revenue equivalence theorem, the envelope argument gives a type's equilibrium expected surplus as $U(\theta)=U(\underline\theta)+\int_{\underline\theta}^{\theta}G(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$. Which two quantities does this formula need in order to give $U(\theta)$ for every type, without solving the format's bidding and payment rules?
options: The win probability $G$ fixed by the allocation and the lowest type's surplus
The equilibrium bidding function and the format's payment rule
The win probability $G$ and the price the winner pays in each realization
The lowest type's surplus and the bid of the highest type $\overline\theta$
